title: Should AI games guide players more instead of giving them a blank text box?
author: MakeEmMayhem
selftext:
Hey guys! I posted a thread here yesterday about whether “infinite content” is the wrong way to talk about AI in games, and someone brought up a point I’ve been thinking about since:

A lot of players aren’t necessarily “architects of their own fun.”

You can give people all the open-endedness in the world, but if they don’t know what to type, what the system understands, or how to get a fun result, they might just have a bad time and bounce off. I think that’s a really interesting problem for AI game onboarding.

“You can type anything” sounds exciting, but a blank text box can also be intimidating. Some players immediately know what they want to try. Others freeze up, type something vague, get a weird result, and leave.

Maybe AI games need more guidance, and help players get to the fun faster.

That’s something we think about a lot with Make’Em Mayhem too. Creating heroes without limits on your creativity is fun, but we still need to help players turn those ideas into something playable and easy to build around.

What do you think? Should AI games give players total freedom, or guide them more clearly into good results?

comments.author: Apalala__
comments.body:
Infinite content means nothing if the experience space is flat. 

The question isn't how much freedom you give players,  
it's how many distinct meaningful experiences your system can produce.

replies.author: MakeEmMayhem
replies.body: Well said! Have you tried any experimental AI games that allow you to do so?

comments.author: OurPillowGuy
comments.body: AI games aren’t a genre, they are a tool. Build and test for what is the most fun.

replies.author: MakeEmMayhem
replies.body: Indeed AI is a tool that helps to expand on current genres. I'm curious to know what are your opinions on what you'd like AI to do for games, e.g. re-imagine a particular genre you enjoy, increase the content you can have a game, etc.
